Abstract Overflow across the Iceland-Faroe Ridge is an important contributor to the deep limb of the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation.
Here, we present results from several dedicated year-long current observations along the ~300 km long ridge crest.
The observations support the hypothesis that overflow is inhibited at both ends by upper-layer inflow of Atlantic water to the Norwegian Sea.

In contrast, retroflection of Atlantic inflow over the central parts, allows the overflow to cross the ridge there, apparently as pulsating flow along two main pathways.

In this work, we present results from ADCPs with temperature loggers and dedicated hydrographic observations from the IFR to address the following questions: Are there locations on the IFR with sufficiently strong and stable overflow to explain the observed features of the overflow jet?
Combined, these data provide robust evidence for the configuration of overflow pathways across the ridge and a holistic overview of IFR-overflow.

With the lack of sufficiently frequent hydrographic data from the water above the ADCP sites, we have not been able to determine typical values for overflow volume transport for the dominant sites or pathways better than within a factor of five.

We can conclude, however, that the two main pathways, together with smaller contributions from the other locations 9 , 14 , may well combine to a total IFR-overflow transport approaching 1 Sv, especially if entrainment downstream of the ridge crest is included.
How these links may be expressed more quantitatively in terms of overflow volume transport remains an open question as do the causal aspects of these relationships.
An alternative approach would be to monitor the overflow jet over the Icelandic slope, although distinguishing between IFR-overflow and FBC-overflow may require additional research.
